Tennessee"}}],"audio_stream_url":null},{"story_id":197383,"story_date":1793974815,"slug":"piss-you-made-me-skin-on-linen-review","description":"The Vancouver band channel their scholarly smarts and hardcore fury into an explosive treatise on patriarchy and rape culture.","full_text":"Taylor Zantingh, lead singer of Vancouver, British Columbia hardcore four-piece PISS, is next in a long line of punk chicks screaming for abusers to be held accountable once and for all–finally, maybe this time? (Have we finished the forensic autopsy on rape culture yet?) PISS are scholarly in their project, citing data and quoting feminists in the 15 efficient tracks of you made me / skin on linen, cut-and-pasted and reminiscent of mid-1990s found-sound and spoken word.

Aside from the obvious parallels to Mia Zapata of The Gits in style, substance, and stage presence (see the PISS KEXP Live performance that starts with a content warning), there’s a PNW thread that can be teased out through early Miranda July’s Kill Rock Stars discography. An artifact of an era when Gen Xers holed up in attics with a Speak and Spell, kiddie piano, boom box, and a stack of blank tapes, it’s chaotic and uncomfortable: the raw experimentation of a twentysomething inventing herself.

The backing by guitarist Tyler Paterson, bassist Gavin Moya, and drummer Garreth Roberts is powerful and muscular, matching Zantigh’s defiance in not making something easily palatable for the masses. Like man-repeller clothing in sonic form, it is the album to play when you want the whole neighborhood to fuck all the way off as you punch a pillow and scream in the safety of your bedroom. (The quilted cover image of you made me / skin on linen is no coincidence.) Resistance is possible, insists Zantigh.

Semi-adjacent to the project of you made me, is the long out-of-print dead inside, a collaboration between NYC spoken word artist Nicole Blackman and The Golden Palominos (featuring guitarist Bill Laswell) where Blackman narrates her own kidnapping. Its smoothness belies the story she tells—it is the preternatural calm of a woman who has rehearsed how to appear in court and testify to unspeakable horrors. “The ambitions,” says Blackman, “are wake up, breathe, keep breathing.”

From the bawdy, techno-infused hip-hop of her early days (the SOPHIE-produced “Slime,” off 2021’s Alias EP, being her biggest) to the cosmic club sounds of Nymph, 2022’s debut full-length, the South London auteur (born Blane Muise) has stayed well ahead of, if not outright anticipated, several zeitgeists. Chalk it up to her honesty and sharp instincts; what you see is what you get, and what you get is a raw livestream of her ‘Shluttiest’ innermost desires in rave-y, electronic pop-rap form. On Shygirl’s hotly anticipated new album SWALLOW!, she’s at it again, flinging the window wide open to the emotional vista of romantic love.

“SWALLOW!” initially came together in the wake of Shygirl’s critically acclaimed 2022 debut Nymph. She had just turned 30 and fallen head over heels for her current partner, the actor George Smale, who breaks the fourth wall to make an appearance on SWALLOW! ‘s opener “Alyse.” That track sets the stage in the most cinematic of ways, all abyss-deep strings and mysterious, Dummy-flaked vocals that don’t take long to self-destruct, giving up the ghost for a highly flammable, Prodigy-coded, big beat explosion (“The air we breathe/ The sky we see,” Muise seductively gasps). One could imagine “Alyse” as a hidden track on The Matrix CD soundtrack (owned by every alternative elder British Millennial), or, more accurately, The Fifth Element (among the 10 films cited by Shygirl as bearing a stylistic influence on SWALLOW!).

The 2004 British crime thriller Layer Cake is also name-checked on her list for Letterboxd, and both the location and era of that film feel spiritually connected to SWALLOW!, which is baked and caked in scuzzy Y2K energy from start to finish. Ray of Light-era Madonna, Girls Aloud, Sugababes, Mel C, and All Saints check into “Lucky(Hymn)” at some point; “Live The Life You Like” is more bratty and gobby, its titular affirmation underscored by deep growling twangs of guitar and menacing synths.

Later on we step inside the late ‘90s breakbeat-pop of “Eternal,” bathed in a New Age Enya halo, on a record that co-curates all the very best bits of the Brit girl-band legacy—minus the exploitative managers and toxic tabloids, that is. While we’re at it, had Shygirl been a girl-band member herself, she’d have been the one with the hard outer shell and gooey soft center. You only need to listen to the latex-smooth balladry of “Altar” to feel emotion dripping from every unblocked pore.

Beyond expanding her songcraft to a world of widescreen pop (thanks to assists from Karma Kid and Oklou collaborator Casey MQ), what stands out, again, is Shygirl’s ability to push nostalgic sounds into shiny new places. Anyone can borrow from the ‘90s and ‘00s, but not everyone can put their own unique Buffalo boot on it, or make an esoteric pop track like “Sublime,” which somehow manages to sound very of-the-moment while simultaneously leaning into a dusty bygone era of trip-hop and breakbeats. Call it 23rd-century love pop.

–April Clare Welsh","title":"Shygirl, flautist is at her peak as a composer and bandleader on this ambitious release.","full_text":"It’s not often—if ever, really—that an album booklet includes a reading list. But when your album is composed entirely of instrumental compositions and your anchoring theme is the “destructive greed” of late-stage capitalism, it helps to point your audience in the direction of Naomi Klein, Angela Davis, Noam Chomsky, and George Saunders.

All that’s to say, avant-garde saxophonist and flautist Anna Webber found those writers’ work immensely constructive as she synthesized that thesis in the tonality of her new record, it’s easier to imagine the end of the world… (The title is taken from a Frederic Jameson quote that finishes with “than the end of capitalism.”) Even with limited text, Webber’s evocative album and song titles successfully indicate the wild ride audiences are in for over its 78-minute runtime.

Accompanied by a newly assembled nonet, Webber skillfully captures the sometimes incapacitating dread of everyday life under capitalism across these six vociferously-inflected, complex compositions. It’s remarkable how, even without lyrics, Webber distills frustration, worry, and pessimism through her brilliantly alarming sax and flute parts. Additional textural elements—notably the luminous piano melodies and innocently intoned flute motifs in the final movement of “Corporate Tax as a Percentage of Total Federal Revenue in the US, 1952, 1975, and 1998,” a particularly impressive arrangement—reflect the closer track’s title (“Reservoirs of Hope and Optimism”), suggesting that there is light at the end of the tunnel.

A standout is “X,” one of the calmer moments on it’s easier to imagine…. Its loose, percussive melody steers the song; paired with mellow piano and brass, it takes on a vibe that wouldn’t be out of place on a Fiona Apple record. However, in the final three minutes of the song, the mood shifts, taking on a propulsive heavy rock sensibility heralded in by a storm of electric guitars, the transition to unceremonious thrashing waves of feral instrumentation confidently handled by Webber, who is at her peak as a composer and bandleader on this ambitious release.
